animation.ops_init: Initialize: write a = {{a}} and b = {{b}} as 8-bit binary, then compute a {{op}} b one bit at a time, starting from bit 0 (the rightmost)
animation.ops_init_not: Initialize: write a = {{a}} as 8-bit binary, then compute ~a bit by bit, flipping every bit
animation.ops_init_shl: Initialize: write a = {{a}} as 8-bit binary, then compute a << {{s}}: every bit moves {{s}} places to the left
animation.ops_init_shr: Initialize: write a = {{a}} as 8-bit binary, then compute a >> {{s}}: every bit moves {{s}} places to the right
animation.ops_bit: Bit {{k}}: a has {{bitA}}, b has {{bitB}}, so {{bitA}} {{op}} {{bitB}} = {{bit}}
animation.ops_bit_not: Bit {{k}}: a has {{bitA}}, which flips to {{bit}}
animation.ops_shift_move_shl: The whole row moves {{s}} places to the left at once: every bit lands {{s}} positions higher, and the leftmost {{dropped}} bit(s) are pushed out of the 8 bits (grey)
animation.ops_shift_move_shr: The whole row moves {{s}} places to the right at once: every bit lands {{s}} positions lower, and the rightmost {{dropped}} bit(s) fall off (grey)
animation.ops_shift_fill_shl: The {{s}} vacated places on the right are filled with 0
animation.ops_shift_fill_shr: The {{s}} vacated places on the left are filled with 0 (a non-negative number shifts in zeros)
animation.ops_shift_none: The shift amount is 0, so no bit moves and the result is a itself
animation.ops_done_not: Done! In 8 bits ~{{a}} is {{result}}, i.e. 255 - {{a}}. Python integers have no fixed width, so ~a gives -{{a}} - 1; that is why the code adds & 0xFF to keep only 8 bits
animation.ops_done_shl: Done! {{a}} << {{s}} = {{result}}: shifting left by {{s}} multiplies by 2^{{s}}
animation.ops_done_shl_overflow: Done! {{a}} << {{s}} is really {{full}}, which needs more than 8 bits; keeping only the lowest 8 bits gives {{result}}, which is what & 0xFF does in the code
animation.ops_done_shr: Done! {{a}} >> {{s}} = {{result}}: shifting right by {{s}} divides by 2^{{s}} and rounds down — the rightmost {{s}} bits are dropped
animation.single_init: a = {{a}}, and bit {{k}} is currently {{bit}}. Every single-bit operation starts by building a mask
animation.single_mask: Build the mask 1 << {{k}} = {{mask}}: only bit {{k}} is 1, every other bit is 0
animation.single_mask_clear: Build 1 << {{k}}, then flip it with ~ to get {{mask}}: only bit {{k}} is 0, every other bit is 1
animation.single_set: a | (1 << {{k}}) = {{result}}: bit {{k}} OR 1 always becomes 1 (it was {{bit}}), and the other bits OR 0 stay the same
animation.single_clear: a & ~(1 << {{k}}) = {{result}}: bit {{k}} AND 0 always becomes 0 (it was {{bit}}), and the other bits AND 1 stay the same
animation.single_toggle: a ^ (1 << {{k}}) = {{result}}: bit {{k}} flips from {{bit}} to {{newBit}}, and the other bits XOR 0 stay the same
animation.swap_init: Initialize: a = {{a}}, b = {{b}}. Three XORs will swap them without a temporary variable
animation.swap_step1: a = a ^ b: a becomes {{a}}. Now a records which bits of the two numbers differ
animation.swap_step2: b = a ^ b: in (original a ^ b) ^ b the b's cancel out, leaving the original a, so b = {{b}}
animation.swap_step3: a = a ^ b: in (original a ^ b) ^ original a the a's cancel out, leaving the original b, so a = {{a}}
animation.swap_done: Swapped! a = {{a}}, b = {{b}}, without any temporary variable
animation.lowbit_init: Initialize: a = {{a}}. The goal is to keep only a's lowest 1 bit, i.e. lowbit(a) = a & -a
animation.lowbit_not: ~a = {{notA}}: first flip every bit of a
animation.lowbit_neg: ~a + 1 = {{negA}}: adding 1 carries through the trailing 1s of ~a, turning them into 0 until the 0 at bit {{low}} becomes 1. Computers store negatives in two's complement, so this is -a
animation.lowbit_neg_zero: ~a + 1: ~0 is all ones, and adding 1 carries every bit back to 0, so -0 is still 0
animation.lowbit_and: a & -a = {{result}}: a and -a are both 1 only at bit {{low}} and opposite everywhere else, so AND keeps just a's lowest 1. Fenwick trees use this to size each range
animation.lowbit_and_zero: a = 0 has no 1 bits, so a & -a = 0
animation.count_init: Initialize: n = {{n}}, count = 0. Each n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so the number of rounds equals the number of 1s
animation.count_minus_one: n = {{n}}, and its lowest 1 is at bit {{lowestBit}}. Compute n - 1 = {{minus}}: that bit becomes 0 and every 0 to its right becomes 1
animation.count_clear: n & (n - 1) = {{n}} & {{minus}} = {{next}} — the lowest 1 is cleared, count = {{count}}
animation.count_done_normal: n reached 0, so the loop ends! {{n}} has {{count}} ones in binary. Since that is not exactly one, {{n}} is not a power of two; the lowest bit n & 1 = {{parity}} tells you its parity
animation.count_done_power: n reached 0, so the loop ends! {{n}} has only {{count}} one in binary, so it is a power of two: a single n & (n - 1) brings it to zero
animation.count_done_zero: n is already 0, so the loop never runs. It has 0 ones, and 0 is not a power of two
animation.subset_init: Initialize: {{n}} elements have 2^{{n}} = {{total}} subsets. Count mask from 0 to {{total}} - 1; bit j set means arr[j] is chosen. Find the subsets that sum to {{target}}
animation.subset_found: mask = {{mask}} (binary {{binary}}) → picks {{subset}}, and the sum {{sum}} hits the target! Add it to the result, listed below the table
animation.subset_done: All {{total}} masks enumerated — found {{count}} subset(s) summing to {{target}}: {{found}}
animation.subset_done_empty: All {{total}} masks enumerated — no subset sums to {{target}}

bit-manipulation-ip-subnet.title: [Networking Basics] How does a router know two computers share a subnet? — A subnet mask is a bitwise AND

sections.content: Every computer on a network has an IP address such as 192.168.1.130. It looks like four decimal numbers, but inside the computer it is a single 32-bit integer, with each part taking exactly 8 bits. The way a router decides where a packet should go is exactly the bit manipulation from this level.

sections.heading: Network = IP & mask
sections.content: An IP address has two parts: the network part says which subnet you are on, and the host part says which machine you are within it. The subnet mask decides where the split falls — /24 means the first 24 bits are 1 and the last 8 are 0, i.e. 255.255.255.0. AND-ing the IP with the mask clears the host part to 0, leaving the network address: 192.168.1.130 & 255.255.255.0 = 192.168.1.0. If two computers get the same network address they are on the same subnet and can talk directly; otherwise the packet goes through a router.

sections.heading: Broadcast address and address count
sections.content: Going the other way, OR-ing the IP with ~mask (all host bits set) turns every host bit into 1, giving the subnet's broadcast address such as 192.168.1.255 — a packet sent there reaches every machine on the subnet. A subnet holds 2 to the power of (32 - prefix length) addresses: 256 for /24 but only 64 for /26. Each extra prefix bit cuts the subnet in half — binary bit weights at work.

sections.heading: Why bitwise operations
sections.content: A router's forwarding table holds thousands of rules, and every packet must be matched against them in very little time. A single AND extracts the network address, with no need to split the IP as a string and compare it part by part. CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) lets the prefix length be any value from 0 to 32, and because a mask is just a run of leading 1s, subnets can be split and merged this flexibly.
